newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood pessimistic over Afghan peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Masood pessimistic over Afghan peace talks.

text.p: With the sound of artillery fire rumbling nearby, Afghan commander Ahmad Shah Masood said on Friday he was pessimistic about peace talks initiated by Pakistan.

The talks, held on and off this week in General Abdul Rashid Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif, are intended to provide a solution to differences between the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, its allies and the purist Islamic Taleban forces they oppose.

"I myself am not optimistic," Masood said of the talks as his Tajik forces, backed since Thursday by Uzbeks loyal to Dostum, traded mortar, tank and artillery fire with Taleban forces near Bagram junction, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul.
Masood also told reporters that in his opinion Taleban troops who captured Kabul three weeks ago have suffered a significant decline in military strength and popularity.

"Taleban is not the same as they were at the beginning. Now they have lost the full support of the people. That is their main weakness," Masood said at his headquarters in Jabal os-Siraj about 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.

The commander from the ousted government said Taleban had suffered 1,800 dead, wounded and captured since they took Kabul while he reckoned his own losses in the last three weeks at not more than 30 men.

The ultra-conservative Islamic Taleban captured Kabul in what Masood, who once served as the Rabbani government's military chief, has branded as a Pakistani-orchestrated effort to undermine Afghan sovereignty and independence for its own ends.
Pakistan has repeatedly denied such charges.
Masood made clear that Pakistan's role in the talks has effectively doomed their outcome.

Referring to a visit this week by a Pakistani delegation to Mazar-i-Sharif for talks with Dostum, Masood said: "My opinion is that the aim of this trip was to divide us among each other and to get some more time for Taleban to get ready (to fight) again."
He noted that Pakistan was represented in the talks not by its foreign minister but by its interior minister, who is alleged by the ousted Afghan government to be a principal backer of the Taleban.
Masood said both Taleban and the government side were using the time taken by the talks to ready for more action on the battlefield should negotiations fail to produce results.
"They are busy preparing themselves and we are also busy preparing ourselves...We are waiting for the results of these talks," he said.
"It (more fighting) will be related to the Taleban's position. If they continue attacking then of course we will have to fight."
Both sides are digging in around the Bagram junction, which controls the main highway north of Kabul and access to Bagram military airfield, where there has been fighting throughout the week.
Despite his pessimism over the talks in Mazar-i-Sharif, Masood said there should be no preconditions for talking with the Taleban.
"For peace we would not have a problem talking to them," he told reporters.
Masood said many Afghans had reacted negatively to Taleban's ultra-conservative Islamic edicts restricting women's rights and forcing men to grow beards and pray at mosques five times a day.
He also suggested that Taleban's reported ties to Pakistan had helped squander much of the movement's popular appeal.
"They (ordinary Afghans in areas recently occupied by Taleban) hate Taleban more than they did the Soviet occupiers in their time," Masood insisted.

He indicated that if the talks produced a cease-fire, the next and necessary step would be for Kabul to be demilitarised so that further talks on power-sharing and elections could take place in the capital.
